title: Viral particles that can be aimed at chosen human cells, given again, and carry large genes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a non-replicating viral gene-delivery platform that combines three capabilities in humans: directing particles to specified therapeutic cell types, delivering an effective second administration despite immunity, and carrying an intact, functional therapeutic cassette larger than a single AAV genome. The objective is to make these properties work together within one vector class, so that targeting, dosing and cargo can be selected for a clinical application. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

AAV illustrates the constraints this platform would address. Pre-existing antibodies can restrict patient eligibility, and antibodies induced by treatment can block subsequent delivery. Its approximately 4.7-kilobase genome also limits the genetic material that can be packaged. That figure is not an allowance for 4.7 kilobases of therapeutic coding sequence: inverted terminal repeats and regulatory elements also occupy space. Loeb et al. demonstrate that immune evasion and engineered muscle-directed delivery can already coexist in a mouse vector, but their work does not establish expanded cargo or the combined human capability.

Selectable targeting means delivering useful amounts of genetic material to specified cells while controlling delivery elsewhere. Demonstrating two target cell types would establish a useful degree of retargetability, not the ability to address every human cell type. Likewise, successful delivery after a second administration would establish a particular dosing sequence, not unlimited reuse. Whether that sequence uses the same capsid or switches between different capsids within the platform is a substantive part of the concept.

significance.text: AAV gene therapies already have clinical applications, but immunity, packaging capacity and tissue delivery constrain their reach. Loeb et al. report that a cited meta-analysis found antibody-based exclusions in 45% of AAV trials. This is a proportion of trials using an exclusion criterion, not a finding that 45% of patients are excluded. If an immune-evasive platform worked safely in humans, it could broaden eligibility for some antibody-positive patients and create additional treatment opportunities after an initial gene therapy.

Additional exposure could matter when an initial treatment produces insufficient expression or when expression declines through growth, degeneration, immune-related vector loss or transgene silencing. Larger functional cargo would expand the genes and regulatory architectures available for delivery. Combining those properties with selectable targeting could make viral genetic medicine more adaptable across diseases, rather than requiring each application to accept the same delivery constraints. These are conditional consequences of achieving the proposed platform.

The revolutionary possibility is a more reusable delivery foundation for genetic medicines: therapeutic designers could choose among target cells, larger cassettes and additional exposures within a demonstrated operating range. Delivery capability alone would not establish clinical benefit. Each application would still require an effective therapeutic design, adequate expression, durability and safety; successful immune evasion would not guarantee eligibility for every patient.

The analogy to a programmable virus is limited to the proposed non-replicating, cell-directed delivery function. A replicating oncolytic virus intended to treat metastatic solid tumors is a distinct therapeutic program. The supplied evidence does not establish that program’s clinical status or determine whether it lacks a single missing virological principle.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the supplied evidence is the integration of effective human second dosing, useful retargetability and cargo beyond a single AAV genome within one vector class. The missing step is not simply to demonstrate immune evasion and altered tropism together: Loeb et al. already combine those properties experimentally in mice. What remains unestablished by that study is their translation to the proposed human platform, together with expanded functional cargo.

Immune recognition remains a concrete obstacle. A capsid that avoids antibodies against an earlier vector can still induce antibodies against itself. Loeb et al. explicitly report that AAV.div3A generates a new humoral response that prevents effective repeat dosing of that same capsid. Their successful secondary administration therefore supports capsid switching, rather than a particle that can simply be reused unchanged. Establishing a clinically useful repeat-administration strategy requires specifying which immune histories and capsid sequences it can accommodate.

Targeting must also translate from animal experiments to clinically relevant human cells. Muscle-directed mouse transduction does not establish predictable human host range, delivery to arbitrary cell types or adequate control of off-target exposure. The study identifies its mouse-only experimental scope as a limitation. A human platform would need evidence that its targeting modifications retain effective delivery under the relevant route, dose and immune conditions.

Engineering synthesis: expanded cargo must mean reliable packaging, delivery and expression of an intact therapeutic construct, rather than merely detecting some material from an oversized input. The integration challenge is to preserve that performance while modifying immune recognition and cell targeting, and to manufacture consistent particles at useful doses. The supplied evidence does not establish a solution to these combined requirements or show that increased cargo can be obtained without compromising delivery or safety.

current_state.text: In their study dated 26 November 2025, Loeb et al. engineered AAV.div3A using a Muscovy duck dependoparvovirus capsid with an AAV2-derived N-terminal domain. In mice, the vector retained transduction after passive transfer of human serum that neutralized AAV9, and it supported delivery after an initial AAV9 dose. Passive transfer of human serum into mice is evidence about antibody evasion in that experimental setting; it is not a human administration study.

The work also produced the muscle-directed variant AAV.div3A-M1, combining an immune-evasive parental capsid with engineered tissue tropism. After initial AAV9 treatment in a Pompe disease mouse model, AAV.div3A and its muscle-directed variant increased GAA enzyme activity. The article reports that AAV.div3A-M1 secondary dosing increased GAA levels ninefold in diaphragm tissue and sevenfold in cardiac tissue relative to a single-dose AAV9 control. These are mouse biochemical outcomes, not demonstrated human efficacy, disease cure or proof of expanded cargo.

The dosing sequence is essential to interpreting the result: the initial vector was AAV9 and the subsequent vector used a different capsid. The authors state that AAV.div3A itself induces antibodies that prevent effective reuse of that same capsid. Thus the study establishes a relevant mouse proof of concept for capsid switching and muscle-directed secondary delivery, while leaving human redosing, arbitrary human targeting and larger functional cargo unestablished.

At publication, the article reported FDA-approved AAV therapies for six diseases and substantial antibody-related restrictions on trial participation. The supplied review supports that attributed six-disease statement, rather than an independently verified inventory of six products. It also confirms that author names are available in the retained Loeb article, correcting the earlier implication that author identification was limited to a PubMed record.

Unverified research lead: the research notes describe a 2025 Ring Therapeutics anellovirus vector, identify a publication in Molecular Therapy Methods & Clinical Development, and attribute mouse eye and brain transduction to it. They also describe it as a first functional vector of its kind and report no established payload expansion or human data. No anellovirus article artifact or PubMed record was supplied for the review, so the company attribution, priority, tissue results, payload scope and human-data statements remain unverified here. This evidence gap does not establish that those statements are false.

The supplied review assessed a retained, untruncated copy of the Loeb article containing the main text, methods and references. Figure images and linked supplements were not inspected; the fold changes above come from the article’s narrative as reported in that review, without independent inspection of the plots. No bounded freshness search was supplied. Consequently, the record supports a dated account of the 2025 study, but cannot establish field-wide absence of the combined human capability as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: show in humans that one defined vector class supports effective transduction after a second administration, can be retargeted to at least two specified clinically relevant cell types poorly served by current systemic AAV, and delivers an intact, functional therapeutic cassette exceeding approximately 4.7 kilobases. Demonstrations should establish these capabilities as properties of the same platform, with the dose sequence and targeting variants explicitly identified. These are proposed milestones, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: One human vector class combines redosing, retargeting and functional >~4.7-kb cargo

completion_criteria.text: Proposed dosing and targeting evidence: distinguish reuse of an identical capsid from switching capsids within the class, document relevant pre-existing and treatment-induced immunity, and establish that the second administration adds useful delivery or expression beyond the first. Define the target cells, route and clinical comparator in advance, and measure target-cell delivery alongside off-target exposure. Mouse reporter or enzyme redosing alone would not meet this human milestone.
completion_criteria.label: Human redosing adds useful delivery with immunity and targeting characterized

completion_criteria.text: Proposed cargo and safety evidence: verify the packaged construct’s integrity and size, explicitly account for terminal and regulatory sequences, and demonstrate the intended therapeutic function after delivery. Establish useful performance at doses without dose-limiting inflammation or genotoxicity during a prespecified follow-up period. Report observed adverse events and the limits of detection and follow-up; an absence of detected harm during that period would not prove the absence of rare or delayed effects.
completion_criteria.label: Intact therapeutic cargo functions at doses without dose-limiting toxicity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the key delivery and second-dose results across independently manufactured batches and an independent clinical cohort or study, with enough procedural detail to interpret failures as well as successes. Define the demonstrated limits in cargo architecture, target cells, immune history, route, dose and duration. Two target types establish demonstrated targeting breadth, and two administrations establish a demonstrated dosing sequence; neither proves arbitrary addressability or indefinite repeatability.
completion_criteria.label: Delivery and redosing reproduce across independent batches and clinical cohorts

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with VIR-01, “A prospective sequence-to-phenotype theory of infectivity, transmission, and escape”: predictive understanding of host range and immune recognition could help design targeting and antibody evasion for VIR-07. VIR-01 concerns general prediction of viral phenotypes, whereas VIR-07 requires a working therapeutic delivery platform with demonstrated cargo and dosing performance.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-03, “Scalable elimination or permanent silencing of persistent viral genomes,” and VIR-11, “An interruptible causal chain from a persistent virus to a major chronic disease”: VIR-07 could potentially deliver genetic tools used in those programs. Delivery would not itself establish elimination or silencing of persistent genomes, identify a causal disease mechanism, or demonstrate that interrupting that mechanism improves disease.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-04, “Protective immunity that covers a viral family, including future variants and unseen relatives,” VIR-05, “Durable immunity at the respiratory surface that stops transmission,” and VIR-09, “A mechanistic correlate that predicts human protection from a new virus”: all involve interactions between viruses and human immunity. VIR-07 seeks to preserve therapeutic delivery despite immune recognition; the other concepts seek broad protection, transmission-blocking mucosal immunity or a predictive measure of protection. Success in one does not establish the others.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-02, “Empiric medicines that cover the major causes of severe acute viral disease,” and VIR-06, “Bacteriophage therapy that can be prescribed as reliably as an antibacterial drug”: these also seek broadly usable treatment capabilities, but address different therapeutic objects. VIR-02 concerns coverage of acute viral disease, VIR-06 concerns phages acting against bacteria, and VIR-07 concerns delivery of genetic cargo into chosen human cells.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-08, “A general experimental reading of viral genes that have no recognizable relatives”: functional interpretation of unfamiliar viral genes could inform discovery or engineering of delivery systems, but it is a distinct experimental capability. VIR-07 would be assessed through targeting, cargo delivery, second dosing and clinical tolerability, rather than through general interpretation of previously uncharacterized genes.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-10, “A single-dose, conditionally replicating interfering particle that keeps a chronic virus suppressed”: both use engineered viral particles, but VIR-10 depends on conditional replication and interference to sustain antiviral suppression after one dose. VIR-07 proposes non-replicating cargo delivery and effective subsequent administration. Replicating oncolytic therapy is another distinct program; neither it nor any supplied roster entry is merged into VIR-07.

unresolved_issues: Whether the combined human capability remained unmet across the field as of 1 November 2026 cannot be determined from the supplied freshness record.
The anellovirus publication’s identity, author details, Ring Therapeutics attribution, priority claim, tissue transduction, payload limits and human-data status require source verification.
The platform’s repeat-administration objective needs a defined boundary: identical-capsid reuse, a finite capsid-switching sequence, or a broader repeat-dosing strategy.
Specific human target cells, comparator performance, functional delivery thresholds and an acceptable off-target profile remain to be selected for a completion demonstration.
The acceptable cargo architecture, dose range, safety follow-up duration and sensitivity for rare or delayed adverse effects remain unspecified.
Figure images and linked supplements were not inspected in the supplied review, limiting independent assessment of the reported quantitative results.

brief.title: Repeatable delivery of large genes to chosen cells
possible: People receiving gene therapy could get another effective dose if the first fell short or wore off. Doctors could use virus particles that cannot multiply to deliver larger working genes to chosen cells, with all these capabilities available within the same family of carriers.
why: This could open treatment to some people whose immunity currently blocks gene therapy. It could also give patients another treatment opportunity when the effects fade.

Larger loads would let treatment designers use genes and control sequences that do not fit in common carriers. Choosing which cells receive them would make genetic medicines more adaptable across diseases.

sources.who: Ezra J. Loeb and colleagues at Duke University
sources.showed: In mice, an engineered viral carrier escaped antibodies, immune proteins that can block viruses. Switching carriers allowed another effective dose, and a muscle-directed version increased a therapeutic enzyme.
sources.quote: In a Pompe disease model, redosing with AAV.div3A or div3A-M1 significantly increases therapeutic GAA levels.
sources.cited_for: This supports combining antibody evasion with muscle-directed gene delivery in mice.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish human repeat dosing, selectable human cell targeting or larger functional cargo.

sources.who: Shireen V. Guide, Mercedes E. Gonzalez, I. Sinem Bağcı and colleagues
sources.showed: Repeated application of B-VEC, a herpes-virus gene treatment, improved wound healing in people with an inherited blistering skin disease. It delivered a gene larger than common carriers can hold.
sources.quote: complete wound healing occurred in 67% of the wounds exposed to B-VEC
sources.cited_for: This supports repeated human treatment with a viral carrier capable of delivering a large therapeutic gene.
sources.not_established: Treatment applied directly to skin wounds does not establish retargeting between chosen cell types throughout the body.

sources.who: M. Peter Marinkovich, Amy S. Paller and colleagues
sources.showed: An extension study followed continued B-VEC treatment in 47 people. Wounds continued to respond, and no new safety concerns emerged; participants and clinicians knew which treatment was given.
sources.quote: No adverse events led to treatment or study discontinuation.
sources.cited_for: This supports continued response and tolerability during extended treatment of skin wounds.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish selectable targeting elsewhere in the body or exclude rare or delayed harms.

sources.who: Muhadasi Tuerxunyiming, Jianguo Michael Yin and colleagues
sources.showed: Researchers engineered a viral carrier that selectively delivered genes to human T cells, a type of immune cell. They also generated T cells that cleared lymphoma, a cancer.
sources.quote: The in vivo generated CD19-CAR-T cells efficiently mediated B cell lymphoma clearance.
sources.cited_for: This supports engineering viral carriers to deliver genes selectively to a chosen human immune cell type.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish the combined human capability of repeat dosing, retargeting and larger functional cargo.

shown: Different carriers demonstrate different parts of the goal. B-VEC already combines repeated treatment and a large therapeutic gene in human skin wounds. It does not establish a carrier family that can be redirected between chosen cell types.

Loeb and colleagues combined antibody evasion and muscle-directed delivery in mice using AAV, a virus used to carry genes. Another dose worked after switching its protein shell. The new shell still triggered antibodies that blocked its own reuse.
missing: A human demonstration must unite effective repeat dosing, selectable cell targeting and larger working genetic cargo within one carrier family.
Targeting must deliver useful amounts to chosen human cells while controlling exposure elsewhere.
Larger genetic loads must remain intact and functional, with safe delivery and consistent manufacturing at useful doses.

milestones.label: One human carrier family combines all required capabilities
milestones.explanation: Human tests would have to unite effective repeat dosing, targeting of two suitable cell types poorly served by current AAV delivery, and intact working cargo beyond AAV’s capacity. This would establish the combined platform.

milestones.label: Another human dose adds useful delivery despite immunity
milestones.explanation: Human tests would have to show added delivery, distinguish shell reuse from switching, and measure immunity and delivery inside and outside chosen cells. This would define when another dose works.

milestones.label: Intact larger cargo works at tolerable doses
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to confirm intact cargo, including control sequences, and therapeutic function without dose-limiting inflammation or genetic damage during defined follow-up. This would establish usable delivery.

milestones.label: Independent batches and patient groups reproduce the results
milestones.explanation: Independent manufacturing batches and a separate patient group or study would have to reproduce delivery and repeat dosing, with operating limits defined. This would establish reliability within those limits.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether useful repeat treatment will require reusing a shell, switching shells or a broader dosing strategy.
The human target cells, delivery thresholds and acceptable exposure outside those cells remain to be defined.
Acceptable cargo designs, dose ranges and follow-up needed to assess rare or delayed harm remain unsettled.

page.title: Retargetable, redosable viral vectors carrying >4.7-kb DNA
page.definition: One class of non-replicating viral vectors, particles that deliver genetic material into cells, carries intact, functional DNA cassettes longer than 4.7 kilobases to different chosen human cell types and supports effective second administration. Retargeting changes particle–cell selectivity; a cassette includes its gene, regulatory elements and terminal sequences.

goal.need: AAV packages an approximately 4.7-kb genome, whereas the COL7A1 transgene is approximately 9 kb. B-VEC's controlled human trial demonstrates a clinical benefit from repeated delivery of this larger gene. Combining that capability with changes in cell selectivity would extend the delivery platform beyond a fixed cellular target.

figures.caption: Complete wound healing at 6 months in GEM-3.
figures.note: 31 participants contributed one matched wound pair each. Open wounds received weekly treatment for up to 26 weeks. Percentages include imputation for missing observations.

statements.body: National Institutes of Health, Somatic Cell Genome Editing programme
statements.quote: Greater capacity and versatility regarding the size and type of genome editing machinery delivered
statements.context: RFA-RM-18-016 lists this among improvements sought in delivery technologies, alongside avoidance of pre-existing immunity and expanded cell-type targeting.

statements.quote: repeat administration as needed to achieve durability of effect.
statements.context: The developer states the purpose of repeat administration in its description of its HSV-1 gene-delivery platform.

completion.title: One viral-vector class demonstrates retargeting, effective second dosing and >4.7-kb cargo in humans.
completion.criterion: Variants of one non-replicating viral-vector class demonstrate changed particle–cell selectivity between at least two chosen human cell populations. In each application, an intact, functional DNA cassette longer than 4.7 kb is delivered, and a second administration adds delivery or expression against a prospectively specified comparator despite the relevant treatment-induced immunity. Both applications meet registered delivery, safety and off-target endpoints. The dosing sequence may switch capsids within the class. Different administration sites alone do not establish retargeting.
completion.set_by: Atlas; no external document identified defines the combined human capability.
completion.basis: Searches covered NIH SCGE funding requirements and TARGETED prize rules, FDA gene-therapy guidance, registered B-VEC studies and developer filings. None defines this combined human test. Two cell populations are the minimum comparison demonstrating retargeting; two administrations establish one redosing sequence. NIH's three-target benchmark concerns genome-editor delivery in animals. Numerical delivery and safety limits remain protocol-specific.

milestones.title: A viral vector reaches its intended cells and produces biological activity in preclinical studies.
milestones.criterion: FDA's proof-of-concept stage establishes target-site delivery and the proposed biological activity in relevant experimental systems. Component evidence includes Loeb et al.'s muscle-directed AAV delivery in mice, with three mice per group in the tissue-targeting experiment. Tuerxunyiming et al. generated functional human T cells in mice; their lymphoma survival analysis included eight mice per group across two experiments. These results do not establish the combined human capability.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Preclinical Assessment of Investigational Cellular and Gene Therapy Products, section III.B.4; nonbinding proof-of-concept recommendations.
milestones.threshold_quote: confirmation that the CGT product reaches the target anatomic site/tissue/cell.

milestones.title: A programmable viral delivery system demonstrates delivery and editing in at least three target types.
milestones.criterion: NIH-supported independent testing in large-animal models demonstrates genome-editor delivery and editing in at least three different cell types, tissues or organs. Evaluation also assesses programmability and efficiency relative to existing delivery systems. This is a published benchmark for the targeting component, specifically for genome editors. None of the cited component studies constitutes this NIH independent validation.
milestones.set_by: NIH, TARGETED Challenge Phase 3b, Target Area 1, requirements revised on 2 July 2025; written for genome-editor delivery.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstration of delivery and editing in at least three different cell types, tissues, and/or organs.

milestones.title: A viral-vector clinical investigation proceeds under an effective investigational new drug application.
milestones.criterion: For the US pathway, an investigational new drug application is in effect 30 days after FDA receipt unless the investigation is placed on clinical hold, or earlier following FDA notification. Applicable investigator and ethics requirements also apply. FDA's preclinical guidance calls for evidence supporting the proposed clinical route and regimen. B-VEC passed this stage: FDA records its IND submission on 20 March 2018 and subsequent first-in-human investigation.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40, with preclinical recommendations in its cellular and gene therapy guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: On earlier notification by FDA that the clinical investigations in the IND may begin.

milestones.title: Repeated viral-vector dosing produces functional therapeutic protein in people.
milestones.criterion: The published B-VEC phase 1 protocol defined molecular correction as functional collagen VII expression and anchoring-fibril formation, structures connecting skin layers. Its phase 1–2 study enrolled nine people with recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa and repeatedly treated matched wounds over 12 weeks. Biopsy findings demonstrated molecular correction. This establishes human function of a roughly 9-kb transgene under repeated treatment, without demonstrating engineered retargeting.
milestones.set_by: Krystal Biotech and Stanford investigators, registered study NCT03536143 and its published protocol objectives; the endpoint was written for B-VEC in skin.
milestones.threshold_quote: to demonstrate evidence of molecular correction, that is, functional collagen VII (C7) expression and AFs, associated with B-VEC after treatment.

milestones.title: A repeatedly dosed viral gene therapy meets its controlled trial's prespecified efficacy threshold.
milestones.criterion: GEM-3 tested superiority over placebo at a two-sided 5% significance level. Its primary endpoint required 100% wound closure without drainage at weeks 22 and 24, or weeks 24 and 26. The 31-person study met this endpoint, with P=0.002. A subsequent open-label extension enrolled 47 people, with median exposure of 81 weeks, and reported no adverse-event-related treatment discontinuations. These are clinical results for a fixed skin-directed application.
milestones.set_by: Krystal Biotech and GEM-3 investigators, registered study NCT04491604; its numerical efficacy threshold was written for B-VEC-treated dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa wounds.
milestones.threshold_quote: only wounds that were healed for at least 2 consecutive weeks were counted as having had a response.

milestones.title: One human application combines cell-selective delivery, effective second dosing and >4.7-kb cargo.
milestones.criterion: A registered human study of one non-replicating viral-vector variant meets its delivery, second-dose activity, safety and off-target endpoints while expressing an intact functional cassette longer than 4.7 kb in its chosen cell population. The dose sequence and treatment-induced immunity are specified. This establishes one integrated application; demonstration of changed selectivity toward another human cell population remains necessary for completion. No qualifying integrated result was identified in the cited studies.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of NIH delivery requirements, FDA guidance and developer clinical programmes found no published protocol defining this integrated human intermediate test.

not_found: No universally accepted numerical thresholds for human cell selectivity, added second-dose delivery or acceptable off-target exposure were identified.
The Loeb full text could not be reopened at PMC or Cell Press.

results.finding: In mice, AAV.div3A-M1 produced 14-fold higher cardiac expression than its parent; n=3 per group.
results.detail: The engineered capsid also increased diaphragm expression and reduced liver transduction. This is preclinical evidence; it does not establish the combined human capability.
results.quote: Incorporating the RGD peptide from an AAV9-based capsid previously engineered by our group, AAV.div3A-M1 exhibited cardiac transgene expression 14-fold higher than AAV.div3A and diaphragm expression 12-fold higher

results.finding: In mice, engineered AAV.div3A-M1 produced 14-fold higher cardiac expression than its parent; n=3 per group.
results.detail: The changed tissue tropism bears on programmability, but the study did not report genome editing or NIH-supported independent testing in large animals.
results.quote: Incorporating the RGD peptide from an AAV9-based capsid previously engineered by our group, AAV.div3A-M1 exhibited cardiac transgene expression 14-fold higher than AAV.div3A and diaphragm expression 12-fold higher

results.finding: In 31 patients, repeatedly applied B-VEC met the primary wound-healing endpoint (P = 0.002).
results.detail: The randomized, placebo-controlled trial assessed complete closure without drainage at two specified visits. The treatment was applied to skin wounds.
results.quote:
Primary wound pairs were exposed to B-VEC and placebo in 31 patients. At 6 months, 
complete wound healing occurred in 67% of the wounds exposed to B-VEC as com-
pared with 22% of those exposed to placebo (difference, 46 percentage points; 95% 
confidence interval [CI], 24 to 68; P = 0.002).

results.finding: After repeated B-VEC dosing, 6 of 8 initially HSV-1 antibody-negative patients seroconverted by week 26.
results.detail: The trial reports repeated dosing and immune responses, but did not establish second-dose-specific activity, intact cassette expression, or the integrated delivery and off-target endpoints required by the criterion.

results.finding: In a 47-person B-VEC extension, no adverse events led to treatment or study discontinuation.
results.detail: The extension had a median exposure of 81 weeks. It was open-label and did not itself test the controlled trial’s prespecified efficacy threshold.
results.quote: An open-label extension study was conducted with 47 subjects (24 rollover from phase III; 23 treatment naïve) receiving B-VEC weekly to target wound areas for up to 112 weeks (median 81 weeks).

results.finding: In 16–19 assessed B-VEC rollover patients, complete wound closure ranged from 61.1% to 89.5% during the extension.
results.detail: Weekly treatment and wound closure provide evidence relevant to repeated dosing. The study did not establish the specified integrated delivery, intact-cassette expression, second-dose comparator, immunity and off-target endpoints.

results.finding: In lymphoma-bearing mice, targeted lentiviral delivery generated functional human CAR-T cells and improved survival; 8 mice per group.
results.detail: The survival analysis combined two experiments. This preclinical result does not establish the integrated human capability.

results.finding: MyoAAV 1A delivered human MTM1 in a mouse model of myotubular myopathy; all 6 treated mice survived through the study.
results.detail: Muscle delivery and transgene expression were also observed. The study does not establish delivery of a cassette longer than 4.7 kb or effective repeat administration.

results.detail: In immunodeficient mice, treated RDEB skin xenografts also showed full-length collagen VII expression. The study establishes preclinical target-site delivery and biological activity, but not retargeting to different chosen cell types.

results.detail: The vector generated human CAR T cells in vivo and controlled leukemia in mice. The study does not establish cassette length, retargeting to multiple cell types, or effective second administration.

results.finding: AAV2 voretigene neparvovec: Phase 1 (n=12) and Phase 3 (n=31) studies were conducted under IND 13408.
results.detail: FDA reports that the clinical studies followed GCP, CFR regulations and IRB rules. A clinical hold occurred on April 24, 2012, following endophthalmitis.
results.quote:
BLA 125610 is supported by clinical data from a Phase 1 study and a Phase 3 study 
conducted under IND 13408.

results.finding: B-VEC, an HSV-1 vector, proceeded to a first-in-human study enrolling 9 subjects.
results.detail: FDA records the IND submission on March 20, 2018 and describes the subsequent Phase 1/2 clinical investigation.
results.quote:
The Phase 1/2 study was a first-in-human, single-center, open-label, randomized, 
intra-subject, placebo (vehicle) controlled study to assess safety, molecular 
correction (PD activity), and preliminary efficacy of VYJUVEK for the treatment of 
DEB.

results.finding: UB-VV111 lentiviral vector: FDA cleared the IND; the Phase 1 study had not yet begun dosing patients.
results.detail: The company expected to initiate the study and dose its first patient by the end of 2024. The source does not establish that the clinical investigation had proceeded.
results.quote: Umoja expects to initiate a Phase 1 study and dose the first patient in the trial by the end of 2024.

results.finding: After a second AAV2 administration, 10 evaluable patients showed improved mobility and light sensitivity through 3 years.
results.detail: The second dose was given to the previously untreated eye. Visual outcomes provide indirect evidence of therapeutic activity, but the study does not report functional protein expression or a roughly 9-kb transgene.
results.quote: Repeat administration led to durable improvement in functional vision, retinal and visual function, and cortical responses.

results.finding: Nine RDEB patients received repeated HSV-1 B-VEC treatment over 12 weeks; biopsies demonstrated collagen VII expression and anchoring-fibril formation.
results.detail: Most healed biopsy samples from seven patients showed full-length collagen VII expression. Mature anchoring fibrils were observed in three patients whose specimens were amenable to immunoelectron microscopy. The study did not demonstrate engineered retargeting.
results.quote: Primary and secondary objectives of C7 expression, anchoring fibril assembly, wound surface area reduction, duration of wound closure, and time to wound closure following B-VEC treatment were met.
